15 Three parallel forces act on an object. As a result of these forces, the object is in equilibrium.
What must be correct for these forces?
A
They all act along the same line.
B
They all have the same magnitude.
C
They do not all act along the same line.
D
They do not all have the same magnitude.

hints: Notice the three forces are parallel, so treat up as positive and down as negative and require the signed sum to be zero for force equilibrium.
Connect that zero sum to directions: one of the parallel forces must oppose the other two, otherwise the magnitudes would simply add.
Compare what happens if all three magnitudes were equal to $F$: check the $3F$ case with all the same way and the $F$ case with two against one.
walkthrough: Equilibrium needs resultant force zero and resultant moment zero. Because the forces are parallel, only two senses along one direction matter.
Let two senses be positive and negative. Then $F_1 + F_2 + F_3 = 0$ with signs, so at least one force must act opposite to the others.
Test the idea that all magnitudes are equal to $F$. If all three point the same way, resultant is $3F$.
If two point one way and one points the opposite way, resultant magnitude is $2F - F = F$, still not zero.
Therefore three parallel forces in equilibrium cannot all have the same magnitude. They do not all have the same magnitude. This is option D.

A.explanation: They can act along the same line, for example $5\text{ N}$ up plus $3\text{ N}$ up balanced by $8\text{ N}$ down, but they can also be offset parallel forces balanced by zero moment.

B.explanation: Three equal magnitudes cannot sum to zero when parallel, since same direction gives $3F$ and opposite directions give $F$ resultant.

C.explanation: They can be offset to give zero moment, but the collinear example above shows they can also share one line and still be in equilibrium.

D.explanation: If all three parallel forces had magnitude $F$, the resultant magnitude would be $3F$ or $F$, never zero, so equilibrium requires unequal magnitudes.
